lectures.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol  (DHCP): Managing IP Addresses on Networks

cues.en: Let's now have a look at how a client can get an IP address.
And in this lecture we will have a look at Dhcp.
Dhcp stands for dynamic host configuration protocol.
And the idea here is that we have a protocol to manage our network and that when a new device logs in,
it gets automatically an IP address by our router or our Dhcp server.
Usually it's running on the router, but it doesn't need to be running on that one because I feel those
slides are always a little bit dry.
Let's just have a look at the problem.
So let's say we got a router or our internet gateway here and here we got one PC already in our network.
Now the next computer is connected to the network.
How does it get an IP address for our network?
So the way it works is that we have a or that we can have a Dhcp server in our network.
It's usually on the physical device called router and but it could theoretically also be another device.
It stores the IP address pool and it manages so called IP address leases.
So a client can request an IP address and then it tells the client, Hey, you can take, for example,
this IP address and it manages that.
They don't that they don't overlap.
Those leases also expire at some point because maybe a device disappears from our network.
Then at some point we want to be able to allocate that IP address again.
So those IP addresses also need to be renewed.
And there's a lot of stuff happening here and this is handled by the Dhcp server in a home network.
This is usually the physical device called router, but again, it can also be a separate device.
Then we go to Dhcp client, it requests an IP address.
So for example, that would be, let's say my phone, my computer, my laptop.
And whenever they connect to a network, they are like, Hey, here, I would like to have an IP address.
Do we have a Dhcp server here in the network that can give me one?
So it's kind of like requesting the IP address and the configuration and it's responsible for periodically
renewing the lease.
Or if we disconnect, then also properly release the lease of the IP address.
We might also have a so called Dhcp relay agent.
We can imagine that if we have like a more complex network with multiple subnets, we have looked at
those before and then we might have a Dhcp relay agent in between that forwards request between subnets
and then that works also over multiple subnets.
Important technical hint Dhcp helps us to manage layer three, meaning that we can easily obtain the
network configuration that we need.
An implementation detail is though that Dhcp is sending so-called UDP packets in our network.
They are technically a layer four or they are a layer four protocol more on UDP later.
We will look at Dhcp right now in this lecture because it really helps us to manage layer three and
well, it's still quite we can still understand it for now.
So we can introduce Dhcp now already.
So what's the process of Dhcp?
The first thing we do is discover that means that the client broadcasts a so-called Dhcp, discover
message and it broadcasts that to the whole network.
So this means that all the computers in our network can listen to it and it broadcasts that to the following
IP address.
This of course doesn't exist, but the way it works is that a Dhcp server would be able to intercept
that message and would be like, Oh, this is a Dhcp request or this is a message I might be interested
in and then it checks it.
Oh, this is a discovered Dhcp discover message.
I need to act now.
So that's how it works.
So the client just sends this discover message to the network to search for Dhcp server.
Other clients will just receive, but just ignore that message.
Then the Dhcp server responds with an offer.
Hey, here I got this IP address available for you.
This message then contains the IP address and lease information and also things for example like subnet
mask and all of this configuration.
Then the client is like, Yeah, okay, here I got hopefully just one offer, but that could be multiple
Dhcp servers in our network.
That's why we need to confirm this that we actually want that.
Then the client is like, okay, let's get real.
And then the client sends a so-called Dhcp request message to the Dhcp server that the client chose.
Usually again, there will only be one, so it will send the Dhcp request to one of them if there are
multiple and it will pretty much be like okay, yeah, here I take that offer.
Then as a fourth step, the Dhcp server will will acknowledge that it will send a Dhcp, acknowledge
message.
And it will confirm that IP address assignment and the lease duration.

lectures.title: The program `ping`: Inspecting Network Connectivity by ICMP

cues.en: In this lecture, I want to introduce you to an important layer three application, the ping application.
We have used that one before, but it makes sense that we dedicate a separate lecture to it to be able
to better understand it.
We can use the ping program to inspect our connection to another computer.
We can use the ping program in the following way.
For example here, ping and then just an IP.
Or we could also ping a hostname or a domain and then the domain would be resolved.
Resolving means it would be turned into an IP address and then this IP address would be pinged.
The protocol that ping works on is called ICMP.
It's the Internet control message protocol.
And our program will send a message.
It's the ICMP message, echo request message to the destination.
And if the destination supports the ICMP protocol, which pretty much all computers do, it should reply
with an ICMP echo reply packet.
Emphasis here is on should because sometimes ping is disabled.
For example, maybe we have a firewall at the other side or in between our connection that disables
those messages and that doesn't let them through.
And in that case we could not do a ping even though it should reply with an ICMP echo reply packet.
Well, if there's a firewall in between, it might be blocked.
It might also be disabled that it doesn't reply that one.
So if we can't ping a host or if we can't ping a certain IP, that doesn't necessarily mean that there
is no connection to that IP.
It just means that through this ICMP ping message, we didn't get a response for whatever reason.
Maybe the other side is down, maybe our connection is down.
Or maybe ping the ICMP protocol has been disabled at the other side or there's a firewall in between.
But if it works, it allows us to easily measure the round trip time to a remote server, which can
give us an idea what kind of connection we are dealing with.
Let's have a look at how exactly that works.
